## The big idea

Shrink the control volume to a point and the ledgers of Unit 5 become
differential equations: continuity and Navier–Stokes. Treat N–S not as
homework to grind but as **F = ma per unit volume** — a map of forces you
can point to in a flow picture: pressure pushes, viscosity diffuses,
inertia carries. Reading that map is the skill; 6.2 turns it loose on
real profiles.

::: {.callout-note}
### The number in charge: Re (again — now you can see why)
Form the ratio of N–S's inertia term to its viscous term and Re falls
out. The number you've computed since Unit 2 *is* the equation's own
statement about which of its terms is in charge.
:::

## Continuity: mass at a point

Take Unit 5's mass ledger and apply the divergence theorem to its surface
integral; since the resulting volume integral must vanish for *every*
possible CV, the integrand itself must vanish:

$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot(\rho\,\mathbf{u}) = 0
\quad\xrightarrow{\;\rho\ \text{const}\;}\quad \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0.$$

For our incompressible world, the whole law is two words: **zero
divergence**. Visually: at every point, inflow and outflow balance — flow
may swirl, shear, and accelerate, but it may not pile up or vanish. This
gives you a truth-test for any velocity field anyone hands you (a CFD
result, a textbook "solution," a colleague's sketch): take its
divergence; if it isn't zero, the field is *fiction* for a liquid. Try
the test:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof field61 = Inputs.select(["shear: u=y, v=0", "vortex: u=−y, v=x", "source: u=x, v=y", "stretch: u=x, v=−y"], {value: "vortex: u=−y, v=x", label: "candidate velocity field"})
```

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
#| echo: false
#| input:
#|   - field61
fields = {
  "shear: u=y, v=0":    (lambda X, Y: (Y, 0*X),   "0        — legal"),
  "vortex: u=−y, v=x":  (lambda X, Y: (-Y, X),    "0        — legal"),
  "source: u=x, v=y":   (lambda X, Y: (X, Y),     "2        — FICTION for a liquid (mass appears!)"),
  "stretch: u=x, v=−y": (lambda X, Y: (X, -Y),    "1−1 = 0  — legal (squeezed, not created)"),
}
fn, verdict = fields[field61]
g = np.linspace(-1, 1, 13)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(g, g)
U, V = fn(X, Y)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 5.2))
ax.quiver(X, Y, U, V, color='steelblue')
ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_title(f"∇·u = {verdict}", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Look hard at the "stretch" case — arrows rush apart horizontally, yet the
verdict is legal, because they crowd together vertically at exactly the
compensating rate. Divergence is a *net* audit, not a vibe; that's why we
compute it.

## Navier–Stokes: F = ma per unit volume

Do the same shrink to the momentum ledger and you get, for constant
$\rho$ and $\mu$:

$$\underbrace{\rho\Big(\frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}\Big)}_{\text{ma: inertia}}
= \underbrace{-\nabla p}_{\text{pressure pushes}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\mu \nabla^2 \mathbf{u}}_{\text{viscosity diffuses}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\rho \mathbf{g}}_{\text{gravity pulls}}.$$

Tour it as a force map, term by term. **$-\nabla p$**: fluid is shoved
from high pressure toward low — the downhill of the pressure landscape
(you've used this since the manometer). **$\mu\nabla^2\mathbf{u}$**: the
Laplacian is a "how do I compare to my neighbors' average?" operator;
viscosity drags every particle toward its neighbors' velocity — momentum
*diffusing*, exactly like heat, smoothing out sharp velocity contrasts.
**$\rho\mathbf{g}$**: weight, per unit volume. And on the left, the
troublemaker: $\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}$ says the fluid *carries
its own momentum around* — velocity transported by velocity. That single
nonlinear term is why turbulence exists, why general solutions don't, and
why a million-dollar prize for basic N–S theory remains unclaimed. (Also
why CFD is an industry rather than a formula.)

Now form the ratio inertia/viscous with characteristic scales $U$ and
$L$: $\rho U^2/L$ over $\mu U/L^2$ gives $\rho U L/\mu$ — **Reynolds'
number is Navier–Stokes rating its own terms.** High Re: the viscous term
is a bit player everywhere except thin layers near walls (Unit 7's whole
premise). Low Re: inertia is negligible and the equation turns docile and
linear (micro-fluidics, lubrication, that 30-micron sand grain from the
drag correlations). The regime habit you've had since Unit 2 turns out to
be *term selection in this equation* — that was the plan all along.

What is N–S *for*, if not hand-solving? Three professional uses: it's
what CFD discretizes (a reviewer who can name the terms can interrogate
the solver's assumptions); it generates the handful of exact solutions
whose profiles you'll read in 6.2; and it's the referee for every
simplified model — Bernoulli, boundary-layer theory, lubrication — each
of which is N–S with named terms deliberately dropped, valid exactly
where the dropped term's regime says so.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
"We can't solve it, so it's useless." Backwards. N–S is the *audit
standard*: every model you'll ever use is N–S minus stated terms, and
every CFD result is N–S plus stated approximations. Engineers who can
point at the equation and say *which term you neglected and why that's
fine here* are the ones trusted with the expensive decisions.
:::

## Earn it — 3 quick gates

A 2-D incompressible velocity field has u = 3x (per second, SI throughout), with v = 0 along y = 0. Ungraded; hints after a miss; **Show me** after two. Arguing about a gate with a classmate is the assignment, not a violation.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-reveal-all"></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Continuity demands ∂v/∂y = ? (a number, 1/s)"
     data-answer="-3" data-tol="0.02" data-units="1/s"
     data-hint="∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0. Whatever x-stretching adds, y must remove — conservation at a point."
     data-solution="∂u/∂x = 3, so ∂v/∂y = −3: the fluid squeezes in y exactly as fast as it stretches in x."
     data-target="dif-s2"></div>
```

::: {#dif-s2 .fl-hidden}
Integrate down from the wall (v = 0 at y = 0):

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="v at y = 0.5?"
     data-answer="-1.5" data-tol="0.02" data-units="m/s"
     data-hint="v = −3y with the wall condition. The minus sign travels with it."
     data-solution="v = −3(0.5) = −1.5 m/s — flow drifts toward the wall as it accelerates along it."
     data-target="dif-s3"></div>
```

::: {#dif-s3 .fl-hidden}
Steady field — yet a particle still accelerates, because its *location* changes:

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Convective acceleration a_x = u·∂u/∂x at x = 2?"
     data-answer="18" data-tol="0.02" data-units="m/s²"
     data-hint="u(2) = 6, ∂u/∂x = 3, multiply. Steady ≠ unaccelerated — the field is frozen, the particle is not."
     data-solution="a_x = 6 × 3 = 18 m/s² — nearly 2g, in a flow where nothing at any point ever changes."></div>
```

Conservation at a point plus convective acceleration: the two ideas that turn Unit 5's big boxes into calculus.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** In fully developed pipe flow (steady, straight, unchanging along the pipe), which N–S terms survive?</summary>
The whole left side dies (steady kills $\partial_t$; "unchanging along
the pipe" kills $\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u}$). What remains:
$0 = -\nabla p + \mu\nabla^2\mathbf{u}$ (+ gravity) — pressure push
balancing viscous drag. That two-term balance *is* Poiseuille flow, and
its solution is the profile 6.2 reads.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Why is momentum said to "diffuse" — what's the honest analogy to heat?</summary>
Same operator, same physics of neighbor-exchange: $\mu\nabla^2\mathbf{u}$
mirrors $k\nabla^2 T$. A sharp velocity contrast smooths outward with
time exactly as a hot spot spreads — and $\nu = \mu/\rho$ has the same
units (m²/s) as thermal diffusivity. Unit 7's boundary layer *is* this
diffusion, given a flow-length of time to spread from the wall.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** Your CFD vendor shows a gorgeous velocity field for water where $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} = 0.3\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ in a region. What do you tell them?</summary>
That their liquid is manufacturing mass at 30% per second, i.e., the
result violates continuity — plot artifact, interpolation error, or a
diverged solve. The one-line audit beats the gorgeous picture.
</details>

## Bring to class

Pick any flow you've seen this week (faucet, creek, coffee stir). Come
ready to name, for one location in it, the *two* N–S terms you believe
are in charge there — and the number you'd compute to defend the claim.
